entries.title: Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong wins NL MVP to cap all-time season of homers, stolen bases and defensive excellence
entries.summary: <p>Pete Crow-Armstrong is the National League’s Most Valuable Player.</p><p>But you didn’t need Thursday’s official announcement to know that.</p><p>All you had to do was be one of the many who marveled at all the 24-year-old <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> superstar did on the field this season to know there was no one in the sport who had as much of an impact as he did.</p><p>“Watching him every day,” starting pitcher Shota Imanaga said through an interpreter in mid June, “he’s a player that overcomes your imagination.”</p><p>Crow-Armstrong has a full trophy case in the wake of one of baseball’s all-time great individual campaigns, just the seventh 40-homer, 40-steal season in major league history with Platinum Glove defense, to boot.</p><p>He’s the Cubs’ first MVP since Kris Bryant took home the award in 2016, the same year his team won the World Series. He’s the 12th player to win an MVP as a Cub, joining legends such as Sammy Sosa, Andre Dawson, Ryne Sandberg and Ernie Banks.</p><p>But unlike all those household names at Clark and Addison, Crow-Armstrong did it in a way that hadn’t been done before. That’s what had teammates in awe all summer long.</p><p>More than the numbers, Crow-Armstrong provided one signature moment after another. He delivered walk-off wins, multi-homer games, a cycle and a memorable night with fellow Chicago sports stars in attendance.</p><p>He also duked it out with Dodgers two-way superstar Shohei Ohtani, the man no one believed could be dethroned from his status as the perennial MVP. That Crow-Armstrong’s win comes in the Ohtani Era is even more impressive, even with Ohtani’s injury issues keeping him from his best self this year.</p><p>For a while, though, there was a real argument that Crow-Armstrong, with his offensive and defensive prowess, matched Ohtani’s impact as both an elite hitter and an elite pitcher.</p><p>“It is really similar to what I saw last year,” designated hitter Michael Conforto, who played with Ohtani in 2025 and Crow-Armstrong in 2026, said in September. “You see a guy go out there and do things that no one else can do. And he does it different than Shohei does it. But it’s the same thing. He moves differently. He has different tools than everyone else.</p><p>“You just kind of enjoy sitting back and watching history being made.”</p><p>It was a remarkable transformation that launched Crow-Armstrong into the stratosphere of baseball’s greats. A guy who chased pitches out of the zone and slumped badly in the second half of the 2025 season was a changed hitter in 2026, his on-base percentage skyrocketing from .287 to .372 and his walk rate shooting up from 4.5 percent to 11.4 as newfound patience made him one of the game’s most dangerous batsmen.</p><p>Add the base-running and defensive abilities that were always there, and the Cubs have a player at the top of their lineup who makes an all-around impact unlike any other in the sport.</p><p>“The most impressive thing is the plate discipline and the walks,” outfielder Ian Happ said in early July. “For him to get to this point this quickly and really … kind of change the way that he approaches at-bats and the patience, the ability to lay off some really tough pitches … that’s been the most impressive thing to watch.</p><p>“There’s always been thump there. There’s always been unbelievable tools and the speed and the defense. … But … to watch the way that he’s walking, it makes him so lethal because he’s such a good baserunner.”</p><p>Crow-Armstrong spent the summer downplaying individual accomplishments, choosing to focus on team goals. At times, he waved away impressive feats, zeroing in on what he could have done better.</p><p>So it’s no surprise that on the night he won the MVP, he was thinking along those lines.</p><p>“In the most humble way I can say it, I still don’t feel satisfied with the product that I put on the field this year,” he said Thursday. “It sounds so melancholy, but I’m so happy being able to say this because I know there’s more.</p><p>“This is definitely a huge accomplishment of mine, this award, but success in my eyes is being called a winner. And I’m not necessarily there yet.</p><p>“Hopefully, I can be talking to you as a World Series champion and MVP.”</p>

entries.title: Finalists for Chicago's next top cop are all CPD insiders
entries.summary: <p>Three high-ranking Chicago police officials were picked as finalists to replace former Supt. Larry Snelling, including a candidate who, if selected, would be the first woman to ever lead the department.</p><p>First Deputy Supt. Antoinette Ursitti, Chief of Community Policing Angel Novalez and Counterterrorism Chief Christopher Papaioannou were the choices of the commission tasked with conducting a nationwide search for the city’s new top cop. </p><p>The Community Commission for Public Safety and Accountability voted Thursday evening to send the names to Mayor Brandon Johnson, starting a 30-day clock for him to make a pick or reject all three candidates and request a second search.</p><p>The city paid national search firm Ralph Andersen & Associates $200,000 to assist the commission. The search drew 46 candidates, down slightly from the 2023 cycle when 53 people applied for the job.</p><p>The applicants included current and former members of the Chicago Police Department, along with law enforcement officials from across the country</p><p>"Having gone through this before, we understand just how much leadership matters," Remel Terry, the commission president, told reporters after the meeting. </p><p>"The right superintendent can shape the direction and culture of the entire department and make a real difference in how public safety is delivered across Chicago. We know what's possible under strong leadership, and we understand what's at stake in getting the decision right."</p><p>Commissioner Angelique Guzman was the sole "no" vote against Papaioannou's nomination. She later said "given current times and the current federal administration," she did not believe he was the best candidate for superintendent. </p><h3><b>Antoinette Ursitti</b></h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-9a0000" name="image-9a0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/67ef7d6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6787x3809+0+359/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb7%2F62%2Fc1f2eb7ac939832ad3316119f2b9%2F7935-x143-4b33-7.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0139c9f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6787x3809+0+359/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb7%2F62%2Fc1f2eb7ac939832ad3316119f2b9%2F7935-x143-4b33-7.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bad3153/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6787x3809+0+359/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb7%2F62%2Fc1f2eb7ac939832ad3316119f2b9%2F7935-x143-4b33-7.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Chicago Police Supt. entries.title: Michael Reese developers pitch $10 billion stadium project to lure Bears
entries.summary: <p>A team of Chicago developers unveiled Thursday a $10 billion, 100-acre development plan for the former Michael Reese Hospital site — both as a Hail Mary to keep the Bears in Chicago and to hit a city-imposed deadline to submit updated plans. </p><p>The Bears previously <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/bears-stadium/2024/05/16/bears-stadium-lakefront-soldier-field-michael-reese-hospital-site-civic-federation-kevin-warren" >dismissed</a> the Michael Reese site, saying it was too narrow and posed safety concerns because the stadium would have to be built over an active rail line.</p><p>But with Capri Investment Group founder Quintin Primo joining GRIT Chicago, the group of developers and investors led by Farpoint Development that purchased the Michael Reese site, the partners have nearly doubled the size of the proposed Bronzeville Lakefront development. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f80000" name="image-f80000"></a> It’s “the key impediment to the team staying Downtown and fairly considering Bronzeville,” Primo said.</p><p>“There should be absolutely no reasons why the Bears and the NFL should not seriously consider Bronzeville Lakefront as the best site for their new home,” he said during a Thursday press conference.</p><p>When asked if the updated plans were shared with the Bears, McLaurin Development Partners founder and CEO Zeb McLaurin said the team will leave “no stone unturned” when it comes to communicating the benefits of the site.</p><p>A Bears spokesperson declined to comment.</p><p>Renderings by Chicago-based design firm Studio Inference show a glassy 75,000-seat stadium that would host the Bears in addition to other sporting events and concerts. competitive dome stadium such as the one we are proposing will outperform suburban locations such as Arlington Heights or Northwest Indiana,” Primo said. “This is just plain common sense, in our Lamont Robinson represents the South Side ward that includes the Michael Reese site, once purchased by the city for an Olympic Village that was never built after the 2016 Summer Games were awarded to Rio de Janeiro.</p><p>“I want to be very clear that before you can remove, tear down Prairie Shores, you have to put the units up first. And the commitment is, before you can bring any housing down, you have to have the new property up. That is a commitment that this developer has made.”</p><p>The developers are also proposing a community benefits agreement that would give "priority treatment for affected households to reside in new housing within the district or nearby, rent protections for five years, additional assistance for longer-term residents and oversight by a resident committee and independent monitor."</p><div The plan cited Lake Meadows as a potential housing site as well as "early discussions" with Illinois Tech to build on-campus housing.</p><p>It also proposed air rights over the McCormick Place Marshaling Yard to the east and expanding McCormick Place's convention and meeting spaces by 300,000 square feet.</p><p>The Metropolitan Pier and Exposition Authority, which owns McCormick Place, said it supports efforts to boost Chicago's economy.</p><p>"However, the Authority must follow its governing mission as well as adhere to its legislatively mandated procurement procedures. The proposed Bronzeville project may offer interesting opportunities for Chicago, but it is in its early stages. MPEA looks forward to learning more about the plans and discussing it with our clients and community stakeholders. At this time, the Authority has not made any commitments related to the project," an MPEA spokesperson said in a statement.</p><p>What sets the development apart from others attempting to woo the Bears, the developers said, is that the new stadium will be joined by hotels, recreational facilities and housing that would <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/11/25/chicago-architecture-center-report-urban-stadiums-development" >bring an economic boon</a> to Bronzeville.</p><p>The developers estimate housing, hotels, retail and commercial uses could generate about $135 million in annual tax revenue. They also project about $14 billion in regional economic activity during its development, with about 60,000 construction-related jobs.</p><h3>Second chance</h3><p>If the Michael Reese stadium plan has a familiar ring to it, it should.</p><p>In March 2025, developers of the former hospital site went public with a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/bears-stadium/2025/03/14/bears-stadium-michael-reese-proposal-scott-goodman" >dazzling Hail Mary plan</a> to build a $3.2 billion Bronzeville stadium and an adjacent mixed-use development — with a great lawn extending over Du Sable Lake Shore Drive all the way to Lake Michigan.</p><p>Scott Goodman, principal of Farpoint Development, acknowledged then that he had not met with the Bears, nor had he finalized the financing for the dome or the $600 million in state money needed just to ready the site for development. </p><p>The previous stadium construction cost, estimated at $3.2 billion, was the same amount the Bears assumed in 2024 when team president Kevin Warren <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2024/04/23/bears-new-stadium-dome-lakefront-soldier-field" target="_blank" >stood with Mayor Brandon Johnson to unveil their preferred lakefront stadium proposal</a> on the Museum Campus — a plan that got stuck in the mud in Springfield and could face legal challenges due to the city’s lakefront protection ordinance.</p><p>Robinson acknowledged the Bears long ago dismissed the Michael Reese site. But he’s all for the idea of including it in the salad bar of Chicago stadium sites for the Bears to consider, along with the site they already own in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/06/bears-stadium-roger-goodell-nfl-commissioner-george-mccaskey-kevin-warren-chicago-arlington-heights-meeting-hammond-indiana" target="_blank" >Arlington Heights</a>.</p><p>“As the alderman of the 4th Ward, I have to develop this site. I cannot leave this site dormant for another 20 years,” Robinson said. “We need more housing, and we need to put this back on the rolls for taxes. The city needs resources and we need housing. As the Bears have stated, they are still looking at sites, and why would we not put everything on the table and have the Bears look at it?”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div We’d be open to having those conversations,” Robinson said, acknowledging the White Sox and the Stars as possibilities.</p><p>Without an anchor like a stadium, Robinson said the Michael Reese development could remain bogged down with another city deadline looming. GRIT has until Dec. 14 to submit an updated infrastructure plan for the site as part of the Bronzeville Lakefront redevelopment process. The development team said it’s preparing a new infrastructure plan to submit to the city and the proposal will continue to be refined with stakeholders, including the Bears.</p><p>“That’s why this plan is out. So many folks can look at it and decide if they’re interested in the site,” Robinson said. “We can’t just do nothing. We have to put plans out there … We gotta develop it. We’ve got to get this thing moving.”</p><p>Bronzeville Lakefront would be a massive public-private undertaking and comes days before lawmakers in Springfield consider financing tools that could sweeten the deal for the Bears to stay in Illinois, making it the perfect time to announce the new plans, McLaurin said.</p><p>State Sen. Willie Preston recalled walking his grandmother to the train, where she’d put in her train token to go to work at Michael Reese Hospital, before urging public officials during Thursday's news conference to act in favor of the Bronzeville site.</p><p>“What you all have created and provided, this development team, is a token to get on the train,” Preston said. “So I’m asking Mayor Brandon Johnson, my good friend Gov. JB Pritzker, the McCaskey family: Take this token and get on the train to economic development ... [and] economic prosperity for the South Side of Chicago.”</p><p>Capri and GRIT's plan envisions a publicly owned stadium similar to Allegiant Stadium, home of the Raiders. Allegiant is owned by the Las Vegas Stadium Authority and was partially taxpayer-funded through a hotel room tax.</p><p>The developers said the Bears could help foot the bill through the sale of stadium naming rights and personal seat licenses, NFL financing programs and refinancing and issuing Illinois Sports Facilities Authority bonds. It would also count on a mix of municipal, state and federal dollars, as well as tax increment financing, sales tax-backed bonds and transportation funding.</p><p>The development team also said it recently signed a memorandum of understanding with "a major capital provider." </p><p>“We have had some very good conversations with capital partners, global organizations, who understand the virtue of how important sports and sports economic development is,” McLaurin said. “We’ve educated them all about the aspects, of the uniqueness of the Bronzeville community, our connectivity, which has been well discussed here today.
